contact_edits.before: Zastrozzi, directed by Jennifer Tarver, is the best time I've ever had at a George F. Walker play, dislodging Panych's Shaw Festival production of Nothing Sacred. Both these works, jokey literary extravaganzas in half-imaginary landscapes, sidestep the credibility problems that afflict Walker's plays set inpresentday Toronto. Zastrozzi is a jaundiced 20th-century lampoon of the romantic 19th-century vision of sanguinary 17th-century Italy: a Revenger's Comedy in which philosophy rules, and kills. Tarver's production impresses from its first moment: a monologue, scared and scary for Oliver Becker as a befuddled Renaissance thug who looks and sounds like Tony Soprano in reduced circumstances. Zastrozzi, "master of discipline," is the ultimate practical critic, pursuing a homicidal vendetta against bad artists; in Rick Roberts's performance, he's a sinner as impregnable as any saint. His particular prey, brilliantly twittered by Andrew Shaver, is Verezzi, a weak-minded painter who also stands accused of killing Zastrozzi's mother. How and why are never quite revealed; and strangely, when the two antagonists come finally face to face (over a heap of corpses), the matter is never mentioned. The play goes down a lot of blind alleys, narrative and intellectual. You can't, in the end, take it seriously; but you can relish it as a young man's high-style high-wire act. The best performance of all, and much his best at Stratford, is John Vickery's as Verezzi's unshakably conscientious guardian, a cropped black wig surmounting a face that's a white mask of determination and despair. - The Trespassers is in repertory through Oct. 4; Rice Boy and Zastrozzi through Oct. 3. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.cafor tickets and information.
